subject: combined-science

items.q: Which description matches a community in an ecosystem?
items.correct: The populations of every species in a habitat
items.misconception: The individuals of one species in a habitat
items.why: In everyday language a community is one group of similar people, so students carry that meaning across and apply it to a single species. The levels of organisation run from the individual organism, to the population of all the organisms of one species in a habitat, to the community of the populations of all the different species, to the whole ecosystem.
items.random_wrong: The living and non-living parts of a habitat

items.q: A gardener sows seedlings very close together in fertile, well-watered soil in an open bed. Which pair of resources will these plants mainly compete for as they grow?
items.correct: Light and mineral ions in the soil
items.misconception: Food and territory around each plant
items.why: Competition is usually taught first using animal examples, and students often call the mineral ions a plant takes from the soil its 'food' rather than materials the plant uses to make its own food. Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.
items.random_wrong: Mates and shelter from other plants

items.q: A disease kills nearly all the insects that pollinate several plant species in a woodland. Which outcome best shows interdependence in this community?
items.correct: Many other species in the woodland are affected
items.misconception: Other woodland species are unaffected by it
items.why: Food chains are drawn as single lines, so students follow the effect one step along the chain and stop, instead of thinking about all the ways species depend on each other. Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. This is called interdependence, so if one species is removed it can affect the whole community.
items.random_wrong: Plants are unaffected as they feed themselves

items.q: Which statement describes a stable community?
items.correct: Species and environmental factors are in balance
items.misconception: Population sizes remain exactly the same each year
items.why: The word 'stable' is heard as 'fixed', and predator and prey graphs are often summarised as 'balanced' without students noticing that the lines keep rising and falling around an average. In a stable community all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant. Numbers still rise and fall, and the species still compete for resources and still depend on each other.
items.random_wrong: The species stop competing for food and territory

items.q:
The table shows the mean number of mayfly nymphs collected at four sites along one river.

Site | Dissolved oxygen in mg/dm3 | Mean number of nymphs per sample
W | 9.8 | 42
X | 8.1 | 35
Y | 5.4 | 12
Z | 3.2 | 2

Which conclusion about an abiotic factor is supported by these data?
items.correct: Fewer nymphs were found where oxygen was lower
items.misconception: Dissolved oxygen is a biotic factor for the nymphs
items.why: Students read 'environmental factor' as meaning 'non-living', so every outside influence, including other organisms, gets labelled abiotic. Abiotic factors are the non-living factors: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals. Biotic factors are the living ones: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another.
items.random_wrong: Nymph numbers are constant in the whole river

items.q:
The table shows the numbers of a predator and of its prey counted in the same community over four years.

Year | Number of prey | Number of predators
1 | 1200 | 30
2 | 900 | 45
3 | 600 | 60
4 | 800 | 40

Which statement is best supported by these data?
items.correct: Prey numbers fell as predator numbers rose
items.misconception: Predators and prey compete for the same food
items.why: Competition is remembered as 'organisms fighting each other', so any harmful interaction between species, including one eating the other, gets labelled competition. Animals compete with each other for food, mates and territory, and plants compete for light and space, water and mineral ions, so competition is for the same limited resources. Biotic factors that can affect a community include availability of food, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and one species outcompeting another.
items.random_wrong: Numbers stayed constant in a stable community

items.q: Rats reach an island on a ship and begin to eat the eggs of a ground-nesting bird. Which biotic factor does this describe?
items.correct: A new predator arriving in this community
items.why: Competition is remembered as 'organisms fighting each other', so any harmful interaction between species, including one eating the other, gets labelled competition. Animals compete with each other for food, mates and territory, and plants compete for light and space, water and mineral ions, so competition is for the same limited resources. Biotic factors that can affect a community include availability of food, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and one species outcompeting another.
items.random_wrong: A drop in the soil's moisture levels

items.q: Camels live in hot deserts. Which of these is a behavioural adaptation of a camel to desert conditions?
items.correct: It rests in the shade during the hottest hours
items.misconception: It has thick fat stored in a hump on its back
items.why: Adaptation is nearly always introduced with pictures of body parts such as thick fur, large ears or long roots, so structural examples dominate what students remember. Adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional. A behaviour such as resting in shade in the heat of the day enables the organism to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives, so it is an adaptation.
items.random_wrong: It makes small amounts of concentrated urine

items.q: Bacteria that live in deep sea vents are described as extremophiles. Why?
items.correct: They live in water of extreme heat and pressure
items.misconception: They live in seawater that is warmer than average
items.why: The best known examples are heat-loving bacteria, and stories about animals surviving harsh weather blur the difference between briefly tolerating conditions and normally living in them. Extremophiles live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles, living permanently in water that is both very hot and under very high pressure.
items.random_wrong: They survive by moving away from the hottest water

items.q: Is an ecosystem the same thing as the community of organisms living in an area?
items.correct: No. A community is the living organisms; an ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
items.misconception: A community and an ecosystem are the same thing, so a community is made up of both the living organisms and the non-living (abiotic) parts of the habitat.
items.why: Both words are used loosely in everyday language to mean 'the wildlife of a place', and pictures of ecosystems usually label only the plants and animals, leaving the soil, water, light and temperature unlabelled. An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment, so the abiotic parts of the habitat are part of the ecosystem but are not part of the community.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do plants need materials from other living organisms?
items.correct: Yes. To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there.
items.misconception: Plants make their own food, so they do not depend on any other living organisms to survive and reproduce.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as the plant 'making its own food', which students extend into complete independence, overlooking that within a community each species depends on other species for pollination and seed dispersal. To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there. Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc., so plants are part of that interdependence too.
